chief_complaint: fever 40.5C, delirium, heart rate 145, history of Graves
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with fever 40.5c, delirium, heart rate 145, history of graves. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: Her husband thinks she caught an aggressive strain of the flu or a kidney infection that triggered severe fever delirium.
concerns: Her husband is terrified that the extreme body temperature is causing permanent damage to her brain.
expectations: Her husband hopes the doctors will immediately bring her fever down with cooling packs and IV medicine so she regains consciousness.

investigation_events.title: Emergency thyroid function tests
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency thyroid function results are now available.

results.note: Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting thyroid tests when thyroid storm is clinically suspected

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thyroid Storm is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a stepwise approach for Thyroid Storm: propranolol, then PTU, then SSKI given 1 hour later, plus hydrocortisone and ICU admission, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thyroid Storm.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sepsis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Extreme agitation with high fever.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Do you have Graves disease, and have you been taking your medication?
Did you have an infection recently?

history.answer: I feel like I am burning up with a terrible fever, and my mind is completely scrambled and racing.
The fever started about two days ago and has gotten dangerously high since this morning.
It has been constantly high and reached 40.5 degrees at home, and I have had severe shaking chills.
I took acetaminophen a few hours ago, but the fever did not come down at all.
No, I do not have a cough, runny nose, or sore throat, though I feel like I cannot catch my breath.
No pain or burning when I urinate, no need to go more often, and no flank pain.
I have had loose watery stools three times today and feel nauseated, but I have not thrown up.
My head is throbbing terribly, but my neck does not feel stiff.
I feel so confused, restless, and scared because I cannot think straight.
No, I have not noticed any rash, insect bites, or black scabs anywhere.
I have been drenching my clothes in sweat and losing weight over the past few weeks despite eating normally.
My thyroid in the front of my neck has been swollen for years, but I do not have any new painful lumps.
No, I have not traveled abroad, done any hiking or farm work, or handled animals.
No one around me has been sick or running a fever.
No, I have never received chemotherapy, steroids, or any immunosuppressive medications.
I do not have heart valve problems or heart disease, and I have not had any dental work recently.
No, I have not started any new medications or over-the-counter pills recently.
I have been in a faithful marriage for twenty years and have never used illicit drugs or needles.
I was diagnosed with Graves' disease about three years ago by my endocrinologist.
I ran out of my thyroid pills about a month ago and stopped taking them, and work has been overwhelmingly stressful.
My heart feels like it is pounding right out of my chest, beating unbelievably fast.
Other than Graves' disease, I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, or any other chronic illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries or previous hospital admissions.
I am not taking anything right now because I stopped refilling my methimazole last month.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, but nothing in the past few weeks.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my husband.
My mother had a thyroid condition, but there is no family history of heart problems or early stroke.
My periods have become very irregular and scanty over the last three months, and there is no chance I am pregnant.
I thought she just caught an awful flu or a severe kidney infection that made her fever spike out of control.

Her body is burning up and she is talking out of her head; I am terrified this fever is permanently damaging her brain. I just need you to get her temperature down right away and give her IV medicine so she wakes up and knows who I am.

exam.finding: Temperature 40.5 C, heart rate 145 bpm and regular, blood pressure 150/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Markedly agitated, restless, and disoriented to time and place, though easily arousable.
Bilateral mild exophthalmos and lid lag present; pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light with normal conjunctivae.
Oral mucosa is dry; posterior pharynx is clear without erythema or tonsillar exudate.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy.
Diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland with an audible continuous bruit over both lobes.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Marked tachycardia with hyperdynamic precordium; regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout with hyperactive bowel sounds; no guarding or rigidity.
Skin is markedly hot, flushed, and diaphoretic without rashes, eschars, petechiae, or wounds.
Supple neck with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Fine, rapid postural tremor observed in both outstretched hands.
